recentItems.title: As Guterres prepares to leave, what can the next UN chief actually do?
recentItems.description:
World leaders are convening in New York for the 2026 UN General Assembly, with the search for Antonio Guterres's successor as secretary-general already under way. The role carries significant symbolic weight but limited executive power, as illustrated by the UN's failed attempts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz despite a task force established months earlier. Guterres invoked Article 99 over Gaza in 2023, prompting a Security Council resolution that was later vetoed by the United States, underscoring the constraints facing whoever takes on what is often called the world's most impossible job.

Al Jazeera's Gabriel Elizondo reports from UN headquarters in New York.

recentItems.title: South Korea's AI boom drives demand for semiconductor trade schools
recentItems.description:
South Korea’s semiconductor exports reached $173bn last year and could double in 2026, driven by surging global demand for artificial intelligence. Samsung and SK Hynix now make up about half of the country’s benchmark stock index, offering annual bonuses averaging $500,000. A growing network of specialised trade schools, including Meister schools, is training students directly for chip factory jobs, with graduate employment rates reaching 96 percent. Enquiries have surged, reflecting shifting career ambitions amid a projected decade-long labour shortage in the sector.

Al Jazeera’s Jack Barton reports from Eumseong County, South Korea.

recentItems.title: Aliko Dangote: Refining Nigeria’s oil, helping Africa, and creating wealth | Talk to Al Jazeera
recentItems.description:
Nigerian billionaire businessman Aliko Dangote says building his refinery was the hardest challenge he’s faced, but he never considered giving up.

For decades, Nigeria - Africa’s biggest oil producer - spent billions of dollars importing refined petroleum products because its state-owned refineries were barely functioning.

Dangote, who is Africa’s richest man, says his refinery has made his country less dependent on imported fuel.

Since the February 28 launch of the US-Israel war on Iran, the facility has seen an increase in demand for its jet fuel due to disruptions to global energy supplies.

Dangote wants to double the refinery’s processing capacity and says he’s listing the company on the Nigerian stock exchange to create wealth for ordinary citizens.

The world’s wealthiest Black man rejects criticism that he’s creating a monopoly. Dangote says his goal is to make Africa great and to make the continent more self-sufficient and less reliant on imports.

recentItems.title: Houthi attacks show Iran's proxies could be 'wild card', analyst says
recentItems.description:
Iran says it has provided the US with a list of conditions for negotiating an end to the war, including ending the conflict on all fronts, including in Lebanon, releasing its frozen funds estimated at more than $100bn, lifting the naval blockade on its ports, and ending US interference in Iran's internal affairs. Meanwhile, the Houthis have launched a ballistic missile towards Riyadh for the first time in their latest escalation, raising questions about whether the US-Iran war and the Houthi-Saudi conflict are now inextricably linked.
Alexandru Georgescu, a military defence analyst and maritime security expert, told Al Jazeera there were "fairly good signals" that the US is considering its military options, with tankers seen on flight-tracking platforms suggesting movement in the air. He said that if the US were to strike again, it would be "more of the same", as Washington has no other major military tools in the region, while the question of what another campaign would achieve after seven months of military action remains unanswered. On the Houthis, he said they could be acting opportunistically but have been "constantly backed up by Iran", including with missile and drone technology, and described them as a prototype for Iran's use of drone warfare and maritime blockades. He said Houthi attacks on the East-West pipeline could indicate "some form of alignment" with Iran's objectives. On the Houthis' claim that they will attack only Saudi-linked shipping, Georgescu said such a guarantee is neither credible nor workable because international shipping involves a "mosaic of jurisdictions" covering cargo and vessel ownership, operators, crews and flag registries. He warned that this could allow the Houthis to target a much wider range of ships while still claiming to have respected their stated conditions.

recentItems.title: How did Yemen's Houthis develop the weapons to strike Saudi Arabia?
recentItems.description:
The Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen, have expanded their military capabilities well beyond their mountain strongholds since seizing state institutions in 2014. Their arsenal, which US intelligence links to Iranian-origin technology, now includes ballistic missiles, drones and hypersonic weapons, claims which Tehran denies supplying. Recent territorial gains near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait have further strengthened the group's control over one of the world's most critical shipping routes.

Al Jazeera’s Ali Hashem reports.

recentItems.title: The 'Naza' outrage in Israel | The Listening Post #shorts
recentItems.description:
The creators of NAZA - a documentary that lays out a system of mass civilian killing in Gaza - have become the target of threats, online harassment and hostile press coverage in Israel.

Elettra Scrivo reports on that fallout and why it’s focused more on the messengers than the message.
